topic: two-phase scheduling is unsafe: a genuine race invalidates the v10 speed result

what_was_built.v10: two-phase: all rows reduce first, per-row scale parked in a shared buffer, then all rows scale
what_was_built.v13: attempt to keep scales in registers (blocked: the TileLang front end turns Python for-loops into device loops)
what_was_built.v14: v10 plus an explicit version annotation on the scale buffer

measurements.v10_rows4_correctness: batch 256/512/1024/8192 all matched float64 (rel 2.8e-4 .. 2.0e-3); 10 repeats at 8192 were bit-identical (max diff 0.0)
measurements.v10_rows2_correctness: batch 128 gave rel 1.0 and was NOT deterministic across 5 repeats; v11 rows=2 failed at 256/512/1024/8192 (rel 1.76 .. 3.95); v14b with a version annotation still failed (rel 23.4 and a NaN)
measurements.v10_gate: one gated window: candidate 0.073269 ms, vendor 0.055201 ms, ratio 0.7519, 15/15 quiet

conclusion: the two-phase shared-buffer construct has a real race, demonstrated by nondeterminism, so it is rejected
the 0.0733 ms candidate time comes from the rejected kernel and must not be quoted as a performance result
the single-phase per-row kernel (v5) remains the accepted prefill candidate at about 0.079 ms
v14 shows that annotating the buffer is not sufficient to make the construct safe
implication: the apparent ~8% win from two-phase scheduling is withdrawn; no partition, scheduling or two-phase variant has yet been shown to beat the single-phase kernel
